note: The interior of a DMN file, as its own subgraph. It imports l2-bpmn -- not for symmetry, but because a DMN genuinely references a BPMN: dmn:usingTask names the business-rule task that invokes the decision. The dependency runs one way, DMN to BPMN, and modelling them as one subgraph would have hidden that a DMN can be read without a BPMN while the reverse is not true of this edge.

groundedIn.what: A real, committed DMN decision table
groundedIn.detail: 1 decision, 1 decision table, 8 input clauses, 4 output clauses, 25 rules, 1 usingTask href into a BPMN. Two of the four outputs serialise as outputEntry and two as annotationEntry; trailing empty annotations are omitted rather than serialised empty, so of the 25 rules 1 carries an L1 citation, 8 carry guidance only and 16 carry no annotation at all. No hitPolicy attribute is present.

groundedIn.what: The L1 reference column WHO's tooling already emits
groundedIn.detail: Its description reads literally "Reference for the source content (L1)". The column is identified by that description rather than by its position, because column order is not stable across DAKs and indexing by it is how this breaks.

groundedIn.what: Data element names embedded in input-expression prose
groundedIn.detail: Names appear bare (`HIV status`) or quoted inside a larger expression (`Today's date - "Date of birth"`). A quoted token is a field or a VALUE depending on which side of a comparison it sits: in `where "Vaccine type" = "BCG vaccines"` the first is a field and the second is not.

valueSets.note: Which DMN element type a column's cells are serialised as. Added by the smart-base migration from smart-kg's propertyNote, which named the two values in prose.

codes.definition: The column's cells are the rule's outputEntry elements.
The column's cells are the rule's annotationEntry elements.

predicates.note: A decision is invoked by a business-rule task. Read from dmn:usingTask/@href, whose fragment is the URL-encoded task NAME rather than its id -- so it resolves only while that prose stays byte-identical in the BPMN, punctuation and the en dash in "Calmette-Guerin" included. Carries a resolutionStatus; the target is a bpmn-task when the BPMN is present and an opaque l1:external-artifact when it is not.

An input clause reads a data element. Recovered heuristically from free text, so every instance carries the extraction rule that produced it and a resolutionStatus. The target is an l2:data-element -- the DAK component -- so a recovered name and a declared dictionary entry are the same class and can meet when a dictionary exists.

A decision rule cites an L1 source. The target is an l1:citation minted from the same string by the citation extractor, so the DMN subgraph and the L1 graph join without either knowing the other exists. Grounded but sparse: 1 of 25 BCG rules. The sparseness is the finding -- a rule with no citesSource edge is a rule with no stated source.

classes.name: DMN File
classes.note: One DMN file as a unit -- the `dmn:definitions` root. Shares its IRI with the l1:external-artifact for the same file, so the l2:decision-support-logic component that points at it and this subgraph name one resource.

classes.name: DMN Decision
classes.note: A `dmn:decision` -- the question being answered, and the node that carries the link back to the BPMN task invoking it. A file may hold several; the BCG file holds one.

classes.name: DMN Decision Table
classes.note: The table realising a decision. Separate from dmn-decision because DMN permits other expression kinds -- a literal expression, an invocation -- and collapsing the two would make the graph unable to say which was used.
classes.propertyNote: hitPolicy is optional and recorded as null when absent, which it is in the BCG table. DMN's default is UNIQUE, but asserting it here would put words in the author's mouth.

classes.name: DMN Input Clause
classes.note: An input column. Its expression text is where data element names are embedded, which is the only reason this is a node rather than a property of the table.

classes.name: DMN Output Clause
classes.note: An output column. The BCG table's four are Care Plan, Guidance displayed to health worker, Annotations and Reference(s). These are column DEFINITIONS in a decision table, not clinical records: no edge from this class reaches an execution artefact, and none may.
classes.propertyNote: serialisedAs is outputEntry or annotationEntry -- DMN splits the columns across two element types and the split is positional, so recording it is what lets a rule's cells be matched back to their columns. isReferenceColumn marks the L1 column, found by its description rather than its index.

classes.name: DMN Rule
classes.note: One row. Its input and output cells are carried as properties, not nodes: 250 of them in the BCG table alone, none the target of a cross-model edge. What the rule needs a node for is its citation edge into L1.
classes.propertyNote: conditions and outputs are arrays of {clause, description, text}. DMN puts the formal expression in description and the human-readable gloss in text, and both are worth keeping -- the gloss is what a reviewer reads and the expression is what an implementer builds.

deliberatelyOmitted.what: A `writes` edge from an output clause to a data element
deliberatelyOmitted.why: No instance exists. The BCG table's four outputs are Care Plan, Guidance displayed to health worker, Annotations and Reference(s) -- none a dictionary element. Licensing the natural mirror of `reads` on no evidence would be inventing vocabulary.

deliberatelyOmitted.what: Nodes for input and output cells
deliberatelyOmitted.why: 250 in one table, none the target of a cross-model edge. Properties of their rule instead.
The BCG table's expressions are prose with quoted names, not FEEL. A parser for a language the files do not use would produce confident results about nothing.
The one committed DMN holds a single decision and declares none. A DRD linking several decisions is exactly what this subgraph should carry when a DAK ships one.
